newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Investors to snap up short-end in Spain.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Investors to snap up short-end in Spain.

text.p: Spanish short-end government debt is expected to outperform Portuguese notes in the coming two weeks, bolstered by expectations for a tame April inflation report later this month, analysts said on Monday.

"This morning we already started to see buying interest in the short end, and people here expect a rally before mid-May similar to the one we had one month ago," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
April inflation, due on May 14, may moderate to below two percent year-on-year and prompt the Bank of Spain to make its fourth interest rate cut of the year, analysts said.
"We can expect the next rate cut as soon as May 16, the following repurchase deal after the announcement of April CPI," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
On Monday, Spain's Treasury sold one-year bills at a yield of 5.30 percent down from 5.347 percent two weeks before.

Although Portuguese CPI is also seen breaking beneath the two percent level soon, dealers expected that market to react "We expect Portuguese CPI to fall below two percent either in April or in May and the Bank of Portugal to push its injection rate, now at 6.30 percent, 25 basis points lower before the end of June," said Manuel Matues, economist at Banco Mello Investment in Lisbon.
Analysts were more divided on the fate of the longer end.

After a positive reaction to the EU Commission report, which said both Iberian countries should fulfil key criteria for joining Europe's single currency, there were analysts in favour of a further decline in yields.

"Let's say in the next 10 to 12 days, the spread (10-year over Bunds) can be back to around 90 basis points for Spain and to around 80 basis points for Portugal," said Valentin Fernandez, chief economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
At midday on Monday, the 10-year spread versus Bunds was flipping around the 100 level for Spain and was at around 88-90 basis points for Portugal.
That compares with a record low of between 83 and 80 basis points hit when euphoria over the two countries' chances to join the single currency was at its height at the end of January.

"When the spread was at around 80 bps at the end of January we had the official rate 50 basis points higher, higher inflation and more time ahead of the 1999's start of the European Economic and Monetary Union," said Fernandez.
"So I do not see why we should not aim for these levels again," he concluded.
But other analysts stressed that a U.S. Treasury sell-off and possible Bundesbank remarks about EMU were hanging over the Iberian market. They suggested a very cautious approach.
A word of caution came from Francesco Giordano, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston, who said that foreign market worries could lift the spread in peripheral markets.

"Domestically, the Spanish economy is doing fine, but the uncertainty of the U.S market and the France election can add pressure pushing the 10-year spread higher to around 110 or 115 basis points," Giordano said.
And other analysts, although convinced that Iberian bonds would offer good value long run, said they were not confident in the trend in the short-term.
"We're expecting the spread to fall to around 70 basis points by year end. But it's hard to say how fast it can move short run," added Matues in Lisbon.
